q: Where does the dependency security policy actually live in the v1.49.0 checkout?
options: deny.toml at the repo root — the plan-era rust-toolchain/ location no longer holds it
rust-toolchain/deny.toml as older docs claimed and still do
Embedded inside .github/workflows as YAML constants
Cargo.lock [metadata] section
explanation: The file moved; the root location is verifiable truth in this checkout.
The policy is a file, not workflow constants.
Cargo.lock records resolutions, not advisory policy.

q: `yanked = "deny"` in deny.toml means a PR whose dependency graph contains a yanked crate will:
options: Fail the Cargo Deny CI workflow until the dependency is updated or justified in the ignore list
Merged with a warning banner on the PR
Only fail when the yanked crate is a direct dependency
Auto-downgrade to the previous non-yanked version silently
explanation: deny level fails CI for the whole graph — warnings are a different level.
The policy applies to transitive deps too; that is the point of supply-chain checks.
Nothing auto-rewrites your dependency graph — humans decide the bump.

q: Reviewing a dependency PR, the immediate signals a goose reviewer checks are:
options: Added via cargo add, lockfile consistent, and the crate does not raise a denied advisory
The crate's GitHub star count and download ranking
Whether the author is in .github/CODEOWNERS
The crate's license compatibility with GPL-3.0 only
explanation: Popularity signals are not review gates in this repo's rules.
Authorship of the PR is not a dependency-validity signal.
No license whitelist exists; the rule is about cargo add + lock + advisories.

q: The Never section of AGENTS.md makes hand-editing `Cargo.toml` dependency entries a blocker because:
options: Human edits desync Cargo.lock and bypass version-resolution review; cargo add keeps both consistent
GitHub refuses diffs that touch Cargo.toml directly
cargo add writes a TOML format cargo otherwise cannot parse
Hand-edited entries run an extra build script
explanation: GitHub has no such filter for Cargo.toml diffs.
cargo parses hand-written TOML fine; the concern is lock consistency.
No extra build script exists; the rule is about consistency, not features.

q: A planted diff adds `get_tokenizer().unwrap()` on a fallible path. Which written rule does it violate?
options: Errors use anyhow::Result — unwrap turns a handled error path into a panic
Never use unwrap in any Rust codebase including goose
rust-toolchain forbids unwrap with a lint that fails CI
The Provider trait requires Result-free methods
explanation: The rule is about error style (anyhow + ?), not a blanket language ban.
No lint denies unwrap workspace-wide in the lints section.
Provider methods return Results; the rule concerns style, not absence of Results.

q: The strongest single blocker among these findings, and why:
options: The parity gap — fixing behavior in agent.rs only may ship a user-visible divergence between the two agent loops
The restating comment — code quality rules make comments reviewable
The missing lockfile sync — CI regenerates lockfiles anyway
The string_slice panic — code style issue only
explanation: A comment violation is real but style-level; parity is behavioral divergence.
No lockfile regeneration happens in CI — consistency is enforced by the rule.
A panic on multibyte input is correctness, but parity compounds the same bug across two universes.

q: Fix this review failure: a reviewer approves a diff that passes tests but contains a hand-added dependency AND a skipped `cargo fmt`. Which gate would have caught each?
options: fmt by just check-everything (cargo fmt --all); the dependency by human review of cargo add usage + cargo-deny CI advisories
Both by cargo clippy alone
Both by cargo test alone
fmt by deny.toml, dependency by the stale bot
explanation: clippy lints code patterns; it does not format or audit dependencies.
cargo test proves behavior, not style or supply-chain policy.
deny.toml audits advisories, not formatting; stale bot handles old issues.
